questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+22t{y}^{′}+50y=0,\,t>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+22t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+50{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+22\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+50{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+22\lambda +50] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+22\lambda +50 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+20\lambda +50 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25) & =0 \\ 2(\lambda +5)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-5.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-5}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-5}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =1.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡x={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}x\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-9x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-9x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-9\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +25] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =5.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=-2$ into the general solution gives

$$
-2={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=4.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5{x}^{4}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{4}+5{c}_{2}{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ and ${c}_{1}=-2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =5{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 4 & =-10+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-2{x}^{5}+14{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =2{x}^{5}(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-17t{y}^{′}+81y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{t}^{9}+{c}_{2}{t}^{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-17t{y}^{′}+81y,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,t>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=0.$ Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =9{c}_{1}{t}^{8}+{c}_{2}{t}^{8}+9{c}_{2}{t}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =9{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 3 & =0+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =3{t}^{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=1.$ Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-7{c}_{1}{x}^{-8}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-8}-7{c}_{2}{x}^{-8}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-7(1)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={x}^{-7}+8{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{1+8\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$

{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-7x{y}^{′}+16y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{4}+{c}_{2}{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-7x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=6,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=2.$ Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=6.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4{c}_{1}{x}^{3}+{c}_{2}{x}^{3}+4{c}_{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2x^2 y'' + 6 xy' + 2y = 0, \qquad x>0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form $y=x^\lambda.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+6x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+2{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+6\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+2{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+6\lambda +2] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+6\lambda +2 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +2 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1) & =0 \\ 2(\lambda +1)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation has a double root $\lambda = -1.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={c}_{1}{x}^{-1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{x}+\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
x^2 y'' - 19 xy' + 100y = 0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y =c_1 x^{10}+ c_2x ^{10}\ln x ,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
x^2 y'' - 19 xy' + 100y = 0, \quad y(1) = 0,\quad  y'(1)=1, \quad x>0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=0.$ Substituting $y(1)= 0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0= c_1.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition $y'(1) = 1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10{c}_{1}{x}^{9}+{c}_{2}{x}^{9}+10{c}_{2}{x}^{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y'(1)=1$ and $c_1 = 0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =10{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 1 & =0+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x) = x ^{10}\ln x .
$$
